raitar = to rule, ruler hevas = secret dantam = only, as in "only Maria knows" ganou = to go down, setting

Yalgai Raitar: Joniu Tam

Ah, yalgai raitar dia*! A nim i ilian-davio e hevas de run tohpu yalgai elemi... En yalen li, run i siyal e dantam oi no elonor oimin cali vardei e ganou lusari. A nim i roesau e yani ciugai en liyar de bale ganter litam, cali a run i ilahai u nim: "A nim i nedas dapas e ganou lusari. O i anifi, nima o i vardei e ganou lusari noli." "Mai a nima i fou i iloi" nim i ilaluan. "Iloi? E ce?" "E ganou lusari. A nima i fou i iloi linu davir li". Notam, run i nomie no nedas iloram. Notor, i asular. Run i ilahai u nim: "Nedas lirul a nim i iliro ca nim en bo!"

*noi, i damura no fanojal de dofa raitar dia (here, it means son of an inherited ruler).

Tips

anifi = come (an)sau = start asular = laughter bale = four bo = home, house ciuga = detail dantam = only, as in "only Maria knows" davio = change, different, turn into davir = right, exact elemi = live, life elonor = peace, calm ganou = down, to go down, setting ganter = ordinal number, rank hevas = secret ilaluan = speak, say iliro = think iloi = hope iloram = surprise linu = until litam = day liyar = morning nedas = 10/10 noi = here, this noli = now nomie = seems notam = first event notor = then, second event oines = laugh siyal = find, notice tohpu = sad vardei = look, see yalgai = small yalen = long yani = new yavuson = slow, slowly

Click to Reveal Translation

English translation:

Oh, little prince!

I came to understand the secrets of your sad little life. For a long time you had found your only entertainment in the calm pleasure of looking at the sunset.

I learned that new detail on the morning of the fourth day, when you said to me:

"I am very fond of sunsets. Come, let us go look at a sunset now."

"But we must wait," I said. "Wait? For what?"

"For the sunset. We must wait until it is time."

At first you seemed to be very much surprised. And then you laughed. You said to me: "I am always thinking that I am at home!"

Here's the second part of the chapter from the Little Prince! See how far you've come :) There will be some things you do not know in the readings to mirror real language encounter. Read it once and see if you can get the gist of it, and then try it again checking the tips below.

Before you dive in, here are a few key words:

heodom = planet helufu = fly, air negafei = only, small amount, as in "only this small thing" coter = number, times

Yalgai Raitar: Joniu Tor

Neloa ilhei i ilian: cali dastor litetan en 'USA, a lusari i anocari en 'France. Daefer run i do i helufu de USA en France en tam litegai, i do i vardei e anocari lusari cali dastor litetan en USA. Bi tohpu, a France a nordau, eta i doum i anye e noi. Mai en run yalgaigai heodom, yalgai raitar, run negafei i fou i anvu e apafene noniu vanpai. run i do i vardei e litam yadetu nehen li ca run i anidai... "Lar" run i ilaluan u nim "i vardei e anocari lusari baledas bale coter! Su yalgai li notor: "A ilhei i eleyel e anocari lusari, cali a tohpu..." "Eta, a run a tohpu?" u run i ilace "noi litam cali i vardei baledas bale anocari lusari?" Mai a yalgai raitar i dacoum.

  • USA = Radom en Wirel-Wilimel. Ilhei ilian ca en noi ledom, i dami muhcar su McDonalds (Country in north-west region [North America]. People know that in this land, there are eagles and McDonalds).
  • France = Radom en Yalgai-Wilimel. A noi ledom a yamirhei caora malvesi su Jenrih Eiffel (Country in small-west region [Europa]. This land is famous for cheese and the Eiffel Tower).

Tips

anidai = want anocari = leave, exit (anocari lusari = the setting sun) anvu = move anye = make, do apafene = sit, chair bale = four baledas = forty (bale + das) cali = when coter = number, times daco = answer daefer = assume, if then dastor = twelve (an)do = can, be able to eleyel = love fou = lack, need heodom = planet helufu = fly, air ilace = ask ilaluan = speak, say ilhei = people ilian = know joniu = piece, part lar = unspecified past, once li = time litam = day litegai = minute litetan = hour lusari = sun negafei = only, small amount, as in "only this small thing" nehen = each neloa = all noi = here, this noniu = some nordau = far notor = then, second event raitar = to rule, ruler tam = one tohpu = sad tor = two vanpai = foot vardei = look, see yadetu = final, finally yalgai = small yalgaigai = very very small

Here, we also have repetition of the root to create an effect of intensity. For example, yalgaigai is very very small.

Click to Reveal Translation

English translation:

Everybody knows that when it is noon in the United States the sun is setting over France.

If you could fly to France in one minute, you could go straight into the sunset, right from noon. Unfortunately, France is too far away for that. But on your tiny planet, my little prince, all you need do is move your chair a few steps. You can see the day end and the twilight falling whenever you like . . .

"One day," you said to me, "I saw the sunset forty-four times!"

And a little later you added:

"You know--one loves the sunset, when one is so sad . . ."

"Were you so sad, then?" I asked, "on the day of the forty-four sunsets?" But the little prince made no reply.

docs.title: JE CLUSTER
docs.text:
Today we will look at the JE cluster! Here's a few words:

Oravia English jelano circle jenai corner, angle jenmue left jenparo front jenrein between jentale through

What do you think JE words are about?

Click to Reveal the Answer

JE words are related to geometrics and locations in space.

🌍 Sound Connections

Tale means cross, through, like Welsh taith (journey, passage). Paro means front. It comes from Latin pro/prae and Romance para, meaning in front, toward.

Here are other words with these roots: boetale = hall (house spaces + cross), just like jentale = through (geometrics and location + cross) varparo = face (face + front), just like jenparo = front (geometrics and location + front)

This cluster has two important words, jetai and jenon.

Jetai means direction, and is used to specify the direction of movement. Compare:

i vanvu en leayo = I run in the park  
i vanvu jetai leayo = I run towards the park

Jenon means path, way. If you use its root in front of a word, you indicate this word as an explicit adverb. Take a look: 

i vanvu yasoi = I run fast  
i vanvu non yasoi = I run fast (way: fast)

This use is an option for when a sentence may be ambiguous otherwise. Notice you may also use a hyphenated expression here:

i yasoi-vanvu = I run fast (fast-run)

You are ready for the reading now!

docs.title: 1. Dropping pronouns and subjects
docs.text:
Oravia omits possessives when ownership is obvious: body parts, family roles, clothing, body actions.

farejor i anifi    = mother is coming (not: my mother)
i siur e yesrel    = remove the jacket (not: your jacket)

Many utterances don't have a subject. In this case, an affirmative sentence defaults to I, and a question defaults to you:

i ilianum   = [V] know-not = I don't know
ce i anye?  = what [V] do? = what are you doing?

In longer sentences or narratives, when a subject is introduced, it becomes the subject until another one is made explicit. If the subject changes, you must introduce it. This is true even if you would normally not use I or you:

Haya i ilian e ca i anye     = they know what [they] are doing
Haya i ilian e ca nim i anye = they know what I am doing

docs.title: 2. Sentence structure
docs.text:
Once a subject is active in discourse, you can use a reduced expression referring back to that subject. This is the full explicit way of saying someone is something:

A Lina a roena dia. A hay a toului.
= Lina is a teacher. She is tired.

But since Lina is already the active subject, you don't have to repeat the full structure. You may say instead predicate + pronoun, or even only the predicate:

A Lina a roena dia. Toului hay.

A Lina a roena dia. Toului.
= Lina is a teacher. [She is] tired.

Another way you may change sentence structure is through moving the order around. To do this, you just need to keep in mind that a marker and all the words it introduces form a block. Each block moves as a unit and should not have its contents split.

nim   i copei   en yamirli bo   en mir lidastor
= I searched in my old house for many years

Example of valid orders:

[en yamirli bo] [nim] [i copei] [en mir lidastor]
[nim] [en yamirli bo] [i copei] [en mir lidastor]

This is NOT valid because it breaks a block:

❌ [nim] en [i copei] nim yamirli bo   (en split from its block)

docs.title: 3. Dropping markers
docs.text:
If you have a clear unmarked block, that block defaults to the subject. Because of this, the a marker is dropped most easily:

a miau i bortal = miau i bortal = the cat enters
a miau e muvardur i copei = miau e muvardur i copei = the cat hunts the mouse

The e marker drops when the object is unambiguous. The u marker is rarely dropped.

Dropping markers and words makes the sentence less formal. Besides this, using roots and short forms also makes a sentence less formal. For example:

a nim i dapas i mo -> formal i pas i mo -> casual

How to Use This Lesson

What do you think HE words are about?

HE words are common tropes in stories and fiction.

There are 3 subclusters. Can you identify which sound is which meaning? . One is about protagonist tropes . One is about antagonist tropes . One is about the cosmos and background

Click to Reveal the Answer

HEI words are protagonist tropes, like fairy and magic. HEH words are antagonist tropes, like monster and ghost. HEO words are related to background, like planet, moon and universe.

In Oravia, you can change the cluster of words, or create new combinations of clusters and roots. For example, the base word for magic is heivio, which is in the subcluster for protagonist tropes. If you are talking about evil magic used by the villains, however, instead of using the protagonist trope, you could use the antagonist trope. How do you think the word would be?

Click to Reveal the Answer

Hehvio.

You may search the full vocabulary page for a few extra words if you'd like to. Do not worry about perfect grammar, aim for clear meaning and expression. Notice that if you write your text here and leave this page, your work may not be saved. You may want to write it somewhere else you can save it. And consider submitting it to Oravia's magazine :) You may choose one of the prompts below for inspiration:

. You are late to meet a friend. What happened? . You help a child, older person or animal . You go to a restaurant, but there is a problem . You see a beautiful thing or place and tell someone about it . Write about a memory that stayed with you . Use these 3 words: leayo, ilotanu, hevas . Use these 3 words: davio, heosu, anivari

What do you think RA words are about?

!!! info "🌍 Sound Connections"
Hucu means command. It comes from Bahasa hukum and Arabic, Hindi, Urdu hukm, which mean law, command, ruling.  
Tai means lead, guide, like Mandarin dài.
Tar means regulate, government, inspired by Arabic and Hindi tartīb.

Here are other words with these roots: antai = leader, to direct (action + lead), just like rastai = politics, politician (society + lead) dohtar = regulation (enforcement + regulate), just like raitar = government (society + regulation)

docs.title: WI CLUSTER
docs.text:
And finally, the last cluster! Here it is:

Oravia English widuo near wilgai village wiltan city wilyel bridge witel map wimlua river wimwa lake wimrih mountain

What do you think WI words are about?

Click to Reveal the Answer

WI words are related to geography.

We also have two subclusters here. What do you think WIM and WIL are about?

Click to Reveal the Answer

WIM words are natural geography and WIL words are human-made geography.

🌍 Sound Connections

Tel means image, like English television and its variants worldwide. Lua means flow, inspired by Arabic lujja (deep flowing water).

Here are other words with these roots: ciutel = image (creative products + image), just like witel = map (geography + image) poilua = current (liquid + flow), just like wimlua = river (natural geography + flow)

We also have four important words in this cluster: Wilimel = west Wirel = north Wiyar = east Winou = south

docs.title: Milestone
docs.text:
Congratulations! You made it to the end of Core!

Before moving on to Expansion, let's see how much you can do.

Below is a conversation between Ana and Kai. They are planning a family meal by phone. This dialogue is more challenging and contains a few words you haven't learned yet, to mimic real language encounter. Try to understand from context first, then check the tips below after reading. You may understand more than you expect!

1. Ana: Eon?

2. Kai: Eon, Ana!Ce run i anye litamis? Nim fa i eodenbor e nim bo.

3. Ana: Oila!

4. Kai: ...Su a nim i fou i boemo u haya.

5. Ana: Run i boemo?Nim i ilianum ca run i do i boemo!

6. Kai: I doum.Caora nim i ilace e run.

7. Ana: Ia, ia.Cei i anvu?

8. Kai: Nim fare, nim fasu su hay falen.Par ilhei.

9. Ana: Su haya i dapas e ce?

10. Kai: I iliro e mocen,mai nim fasu i pasum e moyi.

11. Ana: Eta ilace e run fare!Run i do i ilaluan u hay litam.

12. Kai: I ilacear litamar.Hay i ilaluan ca "e ce run i anye, nim i dapas".

13. Ana: Hmm... a noi daco a yugaium u run.

14. Kai: Ia.Ilie e mogali su moaria molcui?

15. Ana: Kai.A par ilhei i anvu en run bo,su run i anona e moaria?

16. Kai: Ceora um?A moaria a yuba.

17. Ana: Um, nim i do i boemo e elireva mo u haya.

18. Kai: Eloan!Mai a nim boemo a yalgai.

19. Ana: Eta runa i do i anifi en nim bo.Nim i gelna e mo, su i boemo.

20. Kai: Oia, yuba!Nim i anona e gerina u run cali nim i do.

21. Ana: Su celi haya i anifi?

22. Kai: Litamis en alui litetan.Mai a nim fare a yamirli,eta hay i anvu ho yasoi.

23. Ana: Mai i lupupi litamis, dou um?

24. Kai: Nim i ilianum, mai i dami a fare beivu.Eloan!Eta en liperis, nim i boemo u run.

25. Ana: Nima i ilaluan e ca lili en liperis!Bi oi ca nim i eodani e run fare.Hay i do i ilaluan e oimel de run,cali a run a falen.

26. Kai: Oinesum.

Timeline

Based on what Ana and Kai did or plan to do, write a word or two for each time range:

Yesterday:

Today:

Tomorrow:

Next week:

Note

Did you notice yourself scanning for certain sounds to find information? For example, looking for li words to find out about the timeline? The cluster system can help you scan for information faster and easier. This skill will only get stronger in Fluency.

Tips

a = subject marker alui = five anifi = come anona = give anvu = move anye = make beivu = car bi = speaker comment bo = house boemo = kitchen ca = that, which (connector) cali = when (connector) caora = because ce = what? cei = who? celi = when? ceora = why? daco = answer dami = exist dapas = like de = of / from do = (an)do = can dou = or doum = cannot (do + -um) e = direct complement marker elireva = truth, true eloan = thanks en = in / at / on eodani = meet eodenbor = visit eon = hello eta = therefore, so fa = family falen = child fare = parent fasu = sibling fou = need (from anifou) gelna = buy gerina = money hay = he/she/they (sing.) haya = they (pl.) ho = opposite i = verb marker ia = yes ilace = ask ilaluan = say ilhei = people ilian = know ilie = maybe iliro = think lili = again liperis = next week (liperi + -is) litam = day, today litamar = yesterday (litam + -ar) litamis = tomorrow (litam + -is) litetan = hour lupupi = rain mai = but mo = food, eat moaria = apple mocen = chocolate mogali = coffee molcui = bowl moyi = sugar nim = I / my nima = we / our noi = this noli = now oi = fun, entertaining oia = yay (oi + ia) oila = happy oimel = story oines = funny, joke par = three pas = like (from dapas) run = you / your runa = you (plural) / your su = and, with, also u = indirect complement marker / to, for um = no, not (suffix) yalgai = small yamirli = age yani = new yasoi = fast yuba = good yugai = easy

...Su a nim i fou i boemo u haya. ...And I need to cook for them.

Caora nim i ilace e run. That is why I am asking you.

Su haya i dapas e ce? And what do they like?

Hay i ilaluan ca "e ce run i anye, nim i dapas". They said "whatever you make, I will like."

Mai a noi daco a yugaium u run. But this answer it not easy for you.

Ilie e mogali su moaria molcui? Maybe coffee and a bowl of apples?

Nim i do i boemo e elireva mo u haya. I can cook real food for them.

Nima i ilaluan e ca lili en liperis! We will talk about that again next week!

Hay i do i ilaluan e oimel de run, cali a run a falen. They can tell stories about you from when you were a child.

Oinesum. Not funny.

Comprehension

Now let's see how much you understood. Complete these exercises below.

1. True or False? For each sentence, respond IA or UM:

a) Kai knows how to cook. b) Kai's sibling does not like sugar. c) They will eat at Ana's house tomorrow.

2. Sequence Put the events of their plan in order, from earliest to latest:

a) Ana buys the food b) Kai asks his parent c) Kai cooks for Ana d) Kai's family arrives

3. Open Questions Answer these questions in Oravia:

a) Ceora a Kai i anyeum e mocen? b) Cedom haya i mo litamis?

4. Free Production Now write 2 sentences about Ana and Kai:

Answer Sheet

1. True or False?

Click to Reveal the Answers

a) Kai knows how to cook. UM / false

b) Kai's sibling does not like sugar. IA / true

c) They will eat at Ana's house tomorrow. IA / true

2. Sequence

Click to Reveal the Answers

b) Kai asks his parent (yesterday)

a) Ana buys the food (before cooking for the parents tomorrow)

d) Kai's family arrives (tomorrow, three o'clock)

c) Kai cooks for Ana (next week)

3. Open Questions

Click to Reveal the Answers

a) Ceora a Kai i anyeum e mocen?

Possible answer: Caora a Kai fasu i pasum e moyi.

b) Cedom haya i mo litamis?

Possible answer: Haya i mo en Ana bo, caora a Kai boemo a yalgai.

Dialogue Translation

Click to Reveal the Translation

Ana: Hello?

Kai: Hello, Ana! What are you doing tomorrow? My family is visiting my house.

Ana: Happy!

Kai: ...And I need to cook for them.

Ana: You cook? I did not know you could cook!

Kai: I cannot. That is why I am asking you.

Ana: Yes, yes. Who is coming?

Kai: My parent, my sibling and their child. Three people.

Ana: And what do they like?

Kai: I was thinking chocolate, but my sibling does not like sugar.

Ana: So ask your parent! You can talk to them today.

Kai: I asked yesterday. They said "whatever you make, I will like."

Ana: This answer is not easy for you.

Kai: Right. Maybe coffee and a bowl of apples?

Ana: Kai. Three people are coming to your house, and you give apples?

Kai: Why not? Apples are good.

Ana: No, I can cook real food for them.

Kai: Thanks! But my kitchen is small.

Ana: So you can all come to my house. I buy the food, and I cook.

Kai: Yay, good! I will give you money when I can.

Ana: And when are they coming?

Kai: Tomorrow at five o'clock. But my parent is old, so they move slowly.

Ana: But will it rain tomorrow, or not?

Kai: I do not know, but there is my parent's car. Thanks! So next week, I cook for you.

Ana: We will talk about that again next week! I am glad that I will meet your parent. They can tell stories about you from when you were a child.

Kai: Not funny.

Look How Far You've Come

You can now:

  • Talk about family, home, food, actions, time, money, and plans
  • Ask and answer questions about people, places, and time
  • Express what you want, need, can, and like
  • Talk about the past and future
  • Connect ideas, give reasons, and tell simple stories
  • Navigate real conversations like the one Ana and Kai just had
  • Understand most of Oravia with the help of a vocabulary list

Congratulations! You have finished the Core Course!

🎉 Core Complete!

You are ready for Fluency.

docs.title: Milestone 2
docs.text:
Congratulations! You made it to Lesson 40!

Before moving on to the remaining of Expansion, let's see how much you can do.

Below is a short story about Lina and her younger sibling. This narrative is more challenging and contains a few words you haven't learned yet, to mimic real language encounter. Try to understand from context first, then check the tips below after reading. You may understand more than you expect!

Yani Roumir

I dami a yalgai fasu de Lina. A hay a teva lidastor. Lirul en limel, cali a fasu i bonfene, a Lina i roudal e roumir u hay.

En neloa limel, gaomem roumir ca a fasu i anodu dapas: "Be de Miau".

Litamar en limel, a fasu i ilaluan: "Noli nim i roudal u run."

Lina i anona e roumir u hay. A fasu i ansau:

"Cali a lunu i anifi, a miau i anvu en leayo de faejor..."

A fasu i ilaluan e neloa roumir! No yaltan ilhei.

Mai a Lina i vardei: a fasu i vardeium e roumir.

Eta, a fasu i roudalum. Hay i ilian e roumir.

Lina i oines, mai i ilaluanum e noi u fasu.

Litamis, Lina i anona e yani roumir u hay. "Noli roudal e noi."

A fasu i vardei e roumir yalen litegai. Hay i ilaluanum, su haya i vardei e rein. A hay a ho oila.

"Nim i doum!"

"Run i ilian e tam roumir, caora nim i roudal e noi u run neauta lili. Mai run i ilianum canon i roudal. Eta noli nima i ansau."

Noli, lirul en limel, a Lina i roena e fasu. En lunpili, ga lunu, a fasu a yuba.

A Lina i anona e par yani roumir u fasu. A fare a oilaum: fasu i anidai i roudal cali i vil i mo dou anvu en roedom.

Su cali a Lina a toului, a fasu i roudal u hay.

Tips

a = subject marker ando = can anifi = come anodu = the most (superlative) anona = give ansau = begin anvu = move anye = make apasoi = hurry apasoium = not hurry (apasoi + -um) bo = house bonfene = bed ca = that, which (connector) cali = when (connector) caora = because ciude = theme dami = exist dapas = like de = of / from / about doum = cannot (do + -um) e = direct complement marker en = in / at / on eta = therefore, so faejor = woman fare = parent fasu = sibling ga = compared to hay = he / she / they (sing.) haya = they (pl.) ho = opposite, reverse i = verb marker ilaluan = say ilaluanum = not say (ilaluan + -um) ilhei = people ilian = know ilianum = not know (ilian + -um) lili = again limel = evening lipardas = month lirular = custom litamar = yesterday (litam + -ar) litamis = tomorrow (litam + -is) litegai = minute lunpili = spring lunu = winter mai = but miau = cat neauta = ne + auta = level 8, many times neloa = all nim = I / my nima = we / our no = like, as noi = this noli = now norven = already oila = happy oines = joke par = three roena = teach roudal = read roudalum = not read (roudal + -um) roumir = book run = you / your su = and, with, also tam = one teva = six tor = two toului = tired u = indirect complement marker / to, for um = no, not (suffix) vardei = eye vardeium = not look (vardei + -um) yalen = long yalgai = small yaltan = big yamirli = age yani = new yuba = good

No yaltan ilhei. Like a big person.

Mai a Lina i vardei: a roumir a ho. But Lina sees: the book is upside down.

A fasu i roudalum. Hay i ilian e roumir. The sibling is not reading. He knows the book.

Run i ilian e tam roumir, caora nim i roudal e noi u run neauta lili. You know one book, because I read it to you many times over.

En lunpili, ga lunu, a fasu a yuba. In spring, compared to winter, the sibling is good.

Comprehension

Now let's see how much you understood. Complete these exercises below.

1. What do you think? For each sentence, respond IA or UM:

a) The sibling could read before the story began. b) Lina immediately told the sibling what she had noticed. c) The parent was pleased about the sibling's new habit.

2. Open Questions Answer these questions in Oravia:

a) A Lina i roudal u fasu e ce roumir, lirul limel? b) Cenon a Lina i ilian ca a fasu i roudalum? c) Ce a Lina i anona u fasu?

3. Free Production What happened in spring? Write 3 sentences about it:

Answer Sheet

1. What do you think?

Click to Reveal the Answers

a) The sibling could read before the story began. UM / false

b) Lina immediately told the sibling what she had noticed. UM / false

c) The parent was pleased about the sibling's new habit. UM / false

2. Open Questions

Click to Reveal the Answers

a) A Lina i roudal u fasu e ce roumir, lirul limel?

Possible answer: Roumir e ca a fasu i anodu dapas, Be de Miau.

b) Cenon a Lina i ilian ca a fasu i roudalum?

Possible answer: Caora a roumir a ho, su a fasu i vardeium e roumir.

c) Ce a Lina i anona u fasu litamis?

Possible answer: Lina i anona e yani roumir u hay.

Story Translation

Click to Reveal the Translation

Lina has a small sibling. He is six years old. Every evening, when the sibling is in bed, Lina reads a book to him. The book is about a cat that travels in winter.

They have done this every evening for two months. The sibling loves the book most of all.

Yesterday evening, the sibling said: "Now I will read to you."

Lina gave him the book. The sibling began.

"When winter comes, a small cat goes to the woman's house..."

The sibling spoke the whole book. He did not hesitate; he spoke like an adult.

But Lina saw: the book was upside down. And the sibling was not looking at the book.

The sibling was not reading. He knew the book.

Lina laughed, but she did not say this to the sibling.

The next day, Lina gave him a new book. "Now read this one."

The sibling looked at the book for a long minute. He did not speak. He was unhappy.

"I cannot!"

"You can. You know one book, because I read it to you many times over. But you do not know this new book. So now we begin."

Every evening, Lina taught the sibling. The sibling hurried, but Lina did not.

In spring, compared to winter, the sibling was good. Now he reads books he has not seen before.

The sibling has three new books. The parent is not happy: the sibling reads when everyone else is in bed.

And when Lina is tired, the sibling reads to her.

Now he is reading. He does not know this book.

Look How Far You've Come

You can now:

  • Read and understand narrative prose
  • Follow a story across time, place, and characters
  • Understand complex sentences with hypotheticals, habits, comparisons, and negation
  • Recognize extended meanings of words from their cluster roots
  • Express nuance, like what used to be true, what someone knows, what changed

Congratulations! You have reached the halfway point of the Expansion Course!

🎉 Fluency Halfway!

Keep going, you are ready for the second half.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Welcome! This course was designed to give you a feel of how Oravia works and what it is about. By the end, you will know the basics, which is enough to start communicating!

Before Lesson 1, take a few minutes to hear how Oravia sounds and notice one thing about its vocabulary.

docs.title: How to use this course
docs.text:
This course is meant to be light. Read the examples and try the little questions before opening the answers. Keep going even if you forget a word as the same words and sound-meaning connections will come back.

You do not need to memorize everything in each lesson before continuing.

docs.title: Consonants
docs.text:
B C D F G H J L M N P R S T V W Y

Most can be pronounced as you would expect in English or IPA. A few are worth pointing out:

  • C as in cake — /k/
  • H as in house — /h/; /ʁ/ or /x/ are also fine
  • J as in jello — /dʒ/
  • R like the tt in American butter — /ɾ/; /r/ is also fine
  • Y as in yes — /j/

docs.title: Vowels
docs.text:
A E I O U

  • A as in father — /ɑ/
  • E as in cellar — /ɛ/
  • I as in creek — /i/
  • O as in door — /ɔ/
  • U as in flu — /u/

Closed e and o, as in Spanish, work too.

docs.title: Consonant endings
docs.text:
Some syllables end in a consonant. If that is uncomfortable, add a short unstressed i after it:

morta → mor(i)ta

Both are fine.

docs.title: Stress
docs.text:
The preferred stress is on the penultimate syllable:

  • iLIru
  • MOUje

With a suffix, the word keeps its original stress and the suffix gets an additional emphasis:

  • MOUje + UM
  • MOUjeUM

docs.title: Two vowels together
docs.text:
Adjacent vowels are preferably pronounced as one syllable, as in oRAvia, but two syllables are also acceptable:

  • LIria — preferred
  • liRIa — also acceptable

iliru · mouje · moujeum · liria

The recordings may reflect my own accent. Aim for mutual intelligibility rather than to copy an exact accent. Accents vary and there is no "right" accent.

docs.title: One thing to notice
docs.text:
Vocabulary usually takes longer than grammar because words need to be seen multiple times. Oravia gives you recurring sound-meaning connections to help you learn and remember words.

Look at these three words:

Oravia Meaning mihie horse mibeh goat mimu cow

Anything jump out?

Reveal

They all begin with MI.

In Oravia, MI is connected with larger animals. So even before you know the exact word, the opening already gives you a clue about its category.

You will start seeing how this works in Lesson 1.

That's enough vocabulary structure for now. There's more going on inside Oravia words, but it's more fun to let you explore the system as we go.

Start Lesson 1 →

docs.title: Lesson 1: Pronouns and Your First Oravia Words
Grammar
docs.text:
Oravia has three singular personal pronouns:

nim — I / me run — you hay — he / she / it / singular they

hay is gender-neutral. Gender does not have to be marked unless it matters.

Here's something to remember them: nim sounds similar to me, run has u in it, and hay has h like he and she.

docs.title: More than one person? Add -a
docs.text:
Most Oravia words do not change for plural. Personal pronouns are the exception. To create the plural personal pronouns, we add -a in the end.

If run is you, what would you guess for you all?

Click to check

Runa. Add -a:

nim → nima — I → we run → runa — you → you all hay → haya — he/she/it/... → they

docs.title: Possession
docs.text:
Put a personal pronoun directly before a noun:

nim [noun] = my [noun] run [noun] = your [noun] hay [noun] = his / her / their [noun]

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
A lot of Oravia vocabulary is built from recurring sound-meaning pieces called building blocks.

Building blocks make vocabulary easier to learn and remember. As you learn more words, you form a web of associations and an intuitive sense for what they mean. Many times, you may even get a sense of the word before learning it.

Because this is a short course written in English, most of the mnemonics here use English or Romance-language connections. The Complete Course and the Building Blocks page use mnemonics and sound connections from languages around the world.

BOE — rooms in a house. Mnemonic: English bower, a room/chamber. MO — food, eating. Mnemonic: mmm when food tastes good. VAR — face/head area. Mnemonic: visage. DUR — hardness. Mnemonic: durable, Spanish/Portuguese duro.

docs.title: Try boemo
docs.text:
BOE = a room in a house. MO = food.

What would you guess boemo means?

Reveal **boemo** = **kitchen**.

docs.title: Try vardur
docs.text:
VAR = face area. DUR = hardness.

What body part comes to mind for vardur?

Reveal **vardur** = **tooth**.

Notice we don't expect you to be able to guess all unknown words correctly. The point is that thinking about the connections may help you learn and remember words.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown mo food; to eat MO food/eating boemo kitchen; to cook BOE house space + MO food/eating vardur tooth; to bite VAR face/head area + DUR hardness

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
Try each one before opening the translation.

nim boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *my kitchen*

run boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *your kitchen*

haya vardur

Click to Reveal Translation *their tooth / teeth*

nim mo

Click to Reveal Translation *my food*

docs.title: Your turn
docs.text: Write our food, your kitchen, and their tooth / teeth.

docs.title: Mini Review
docs.text:
Quick review:

Continue to Lesson 2 →

docs.title: Lesson 2: A & I Markers
docs.text: Last lesson, mo meant food. The same word can also mean eat. So how do you know which one you are looking at?

docs.title: i tells you: this is the action
docs.text:
Put i before a word when it is being used as a verb:

i mo

Now add the person doing it.

a marks the subject, as in A = Actor. i marks the verb, as in I = Initiates.

The pattern is:

a [subject] i [verb]

a nim i mo

Click to Reveal Translation *I eat.*

With a simple pronoun, a is very often left out in ordinary speech:

nim i mo

Click to Reveal Translation *I eat.*

In a short utterance about yourself, nim is often left out too:

i mo

Click to Reveal Translation *I eat.*

So all three occur:

a nim i mo → nim i mo → i mo

In conversation, i mo can simply mean “I'm eating.” Nim is used to make the subject explicit.

docs.title: Clusters: the semantic domain
docs.text:
Last lesson you saw boemo “kitchen”:

BOE + MO → house space + food/eating → kitchen

The opening part is especially important. A cluster is a semantic domain, it tells you what kind of thing or idea the word is. Other building blocks add associations inside that domain.

For example, BOE tells you that boemo is a house-space concept. MO connects it with food/eating.

If a word starts with AN, expect an action. YAL points to size and dimensions. You already know VAR, the face/head area, from Lesson 1. And so on.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: AN — action. Mnemonic: AN action. VU — movement. Mnemonic: Velocity, underway. YAL — size and dimension. Mnemonic: a yard measures size. GAI — small. Mnemonic: a tiny grain.

docs.title: Try varmo
docs.text:
You already know both pieces from Lesson 1:

VAR = face/head area. MO = food/eating.

What body part comes to mind for varmo?

Reveal **varmo** = **mouth**.

Now compare:

boemo = house room + food/eating → kitchen varmo = face/head area + food/eating → mouth

The shared MO creates an association and gives you a clue. And the opening cluster tells you what semantic domain the word belongs to.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown anvu move, go AN action + VU movement yalgai small YAL size + GAI small varmo mouth VAR face/head area + MO eating

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From Lesson 1

mo = eat / food boemo = kitchen / cook

a nim i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I go.*

a hay i mo

Click to Reveal Translation *They eat.*

run varmo

Click to Reveal Translation *your mouth*

docs.title: Your turn
docs.text: Write one sentence with nim or hay, then write one sentence about yourself without nim.

docs.title: Mini Review
docs.text:
Quick review:

Continue to Lesson 3 →

docs.title: Want to negate something? Add -um
docs.text:
Attach -um to the word you want to negate.

i mo → i moum

Click to Reveal Translation *I eat → I do not eat.*

The same suffix can negate other kinds of words besides verbs:

yalgai = small → yalgaium = not small boemo = kitchen → boemoum = not a kitchen

docs.title: Modifiers come before what they modify
docs.text:
yalgai boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *small kitchen*

The same order also explains the possessive phrases from Lesson 1: in nim boemo, nim narrows which kitchen you mean.

docs.title: Words are flexible
docs.text:
A word does not need a different noun, verb, and adjective form every time its role changes.

boemo = kitchen i boemo = to cook

mo = food i mo = to eat

The markers and sentence structure tell you how the concept is being used.

docs.title: Roots: connections across clusters
docs.text:
A root usually comes after the opening cluster. Unlike a cluster, it can show up across very different kinds of words.

Compare:

anvu = AN action + VU movement → move / go beivu = BEI vehicle + VU movement → drive / car

AN tells you that anvu is an action. BEI tells you that beivu is a vehicle. Both end in VU, movement.

You have already seen the same pattern with DUR:

vardur = VAR face/head area + DUR hardness → tooth yudur = YU subjective quality + DUR hardness → hard / difficult

The opening cluster gives the broad semantic domain of the word. The root adds another association.

That helps explain a word like eofa:

eofa = EO social relationships + FA family → friend

Because EO is the opening cluster, eofa belongs to the social-relationship domain. FA adds the association with family or closeness.

Just as with clusters, roots are clues meant to help learning, and they may not always be exact science. If an association makes sense to you, use it. It may help you remember the word.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: BEI — vehicles. Mnemonic: be in a vehicle. EO — social relationships. Mnemonic: Each Other. FA — family. Mnemonic: family / familia / família. YU — subjective qualities. Mnemonic: how YOU experience it. LEI — plants. Mnemonic: leaf. RIH — higher, rising. Mnemonic: RIse High. APA — physical movement. Mnemonic: A Physical Action.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown beivu car, to drive BEI vehicles + VU movement eofa friend EO social relationships + FA family yudur hard, difficult YU subjective quality + DUR hardness leirih tree LEI plants + RIH rising aparih jump APA physical movement + RIH rising

docs.title: Spot the connections
docs.text:
Compare vardur / yudur and leirih / aparih. What repeats?

Reveal

DUR = hardness, connecting vardur “tooth” and yudur “difficult/hard.” RIH = rising, connecting leirih “tree” and aparih “jump.”

The same idea appeared in eofa: the opening EO gives the broad social domain, while FA gives another semantic clue.

docs.text:
From earlier lessons

mo = eat / food boemo = kitchen / cook yalgai = small

i moum

Click to Reveal Translation *I do not eat.*

nim eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *my friend*

nim beivu

Click to Reveal Translation *my car*

yalgai eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *small friend / a small friend*

i aparih

Click to Reveal Translation *I jump.*

yudur aparih

Click to Reveal Translation *a difficult jump*

i boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *I cook.*

docs.title: Lesson 4: E Marker and the Copula
docs.text: You can already say i mo “I eat.” But eat what?

docs.title: E marks what the action engages
docs.text:
Add e for the direct object.

You now have:

A = Actor I = Initiates E = Engaging

The basic pattern is:

a [subject] i [verb] e [object]

nim i mo e mo

Click to Reveal Translation *I eat food.*

The e tells you that the second mo — food — is the direct object.

docs.title: Saying “is” without a separate word for “is”
docs.text:
For ordinary identity and description, Oravia does not insert a separate am / is / are verb. We use a on both sides:

a [subject] a [description or identity]

Before looking at an example, try it yourself.

You already know leirih = tree and yalgai = small. How would you say The tree is small?

Reveal `a leirih a yalgai` *The tree is small.*

That's it: the second a introduces the identity or description.

docs.title: Objective and subjective qualities
docs.text:
Oravia separates two broad kinds of qualities:

YAL — measurable size/dimension: small, long, wide, and so on YU — subjective qualities: easy, difficult, pleasant, and so on

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: TAN — big. Mnemonic: a Titan is huge. ELE — self-expansion, flourishing. Mnemonic: elevate. YEL — joining. Mnemonic: think of a yoke joining two things. VI — inside the body. Mnemonic: viscera. WA — water, sea. Mnemonic: water. MU — small animals. Mnemonic: a mouse is a small animal.

docs.title: Try vidur
docs.text:
You already know DUR = hardness from Lesson 1.

VI = inside the body. DUR = hardness.

What body material comes to mind for vidur?

Reveal **vidur** = **bone**.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown yaltan big, large YAL size + TAN big eleyel love ELE self-expansion + YEL joining wamu fish WA water + MU small animal vidur bone VI inside the body + DUR hardness viwa blood VI inside the body + WA water/liquid yugai easy YU subjective quality + GAI small

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

eofa = friend leirih = tree yudur = hard / difficult aparih = jump

nim i eleyel e nim eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I love my friend.*

a leirih a yaltan

Click to Reveal Translation *The tree is big.*

a vidur a yudur

Click to Reveal Translation *Bone is hard.*

a wamu a yalgai

Click to Reveal Translation *The fish is small.*

a aparih a yugai

Click to Reveal Translation *Jumping is easy.*

docs.title: Lesson 5: U Marker, De, En
docs.text: Suppose you say I give the food. The obvious next question is: to whom?

docs.title: U: to / for
docs.text:
That recipient gets u:

u — indirect object, usually to or for. Mnemonic: U = Unto.

For the example below, anona means give. Its breakdown comes later in the lesson.

Now the whole mnemonic finally fits:

Actor Initiates, Engaging, Unto.

Marker Mnemonic Main role a Actor subject i Initiates verb e Engaging direct object u Unto indirect object: to / for

a nim i anona e mo u eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I give food to a friend.*

Because the markers show the roles, Oravia has flexible word order. Other orders are just as acceptable, and speakers can choose the one that feels comfortable or matches the style they want to use. In this short English-language course, most examples follow English-like order to keep it simple.

docs.title: De: of / from
docs.text:
de connects something to a source, origin, or possessor:

boemo de eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *the friend's kitchen / the kitchen of the friend*

Personal pronouns still use the shorter pattern from Lesson 1:

nim boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *my kitchen*

It may help you remember to think of Romance de.

docs.title: En: in / on / at
docs.text:
en covers ordinary location and time relations such as in, on, and at:

nim en boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *I am in the kitchen.*

bo means house / home.

nim en bo

Click to Reveal Translation *I am at home.*

Notice that there is no a ... a ... here (is/are), because en already expresses the location.

To remember, think about en being similar to in, or Spanish en.

docs.title: How much do you actually have to mark?
docs.text: In ordinary speech, markers may be dropped, as you already saw with a nim i mo → nim i mo. Use a marker whenever it helps make the role clear.

docs.title: Subclusters: a narrower kind of thing
docs.text:
A cluster says what general kind of thing is this? A subcluster zooms in one step further.

The AN family makes it easy to see:

AN — action in general ANE — static action: staying, resting, remaining ANI — movement toward ANO — movement away

So to keep this in mind: ANI- points toward, and ANO- points away.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: ANE — static action. Mnemonic: E = at Ease, staying in place. FENE — rest. Mnemonic: FINish, then rest. ANO — movement away. Mnemonic: O = Out. NA — giving. Mnemonic: “Now, Accept this.” BOR — structural parts of a house. Mnemonic: the border of the house. LU — outside. Mnemonic: Look Up when you are outside.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown anefene rest ANE static action + FENE rest anona give ANO movement away + NA giving borlu window BOR house structure + LU outside leigai shrub LEI plants + GAI small vardur tooth VAR face/head area + DUR hardness

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

viwa = blood boemo = kitchen / cook yudur = hard / difficult yalgai = small

i anona e mo u eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I give food to a friend.*

i anona e viwa

Click to Reveal Translation *I give / donate blood.*

a borlu de boemo a yalgai

Click to Reveal Translation *The kitchen window is small.*

a vardur a yudur

Click to Reveal Translation *The tooth is hard.*

i anefene en boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *I rest in the kitchen.*

a leigai a yalgai

Click to Reveal Translation *The shrub is small.*

docs.title: Yes/no questions: change the intonation
docs.text:
For a yes/no question, the words can stay the same. You may end the question with ia (yes), or um (no).

When you're speaking directly to someone, run is usually unnecessary:

i anvu?

Click to Reveal Translation *Are you going?*

Notice this is the same as i anvu, ia?

docs.title: CE: “what?”
docs.text:
ce means what?, like que in Romance languages. For example:

ce i mo? / e ce i mo? means what are you eating?

The question word being in the beginning is not mandatory, as the order is flexible:

i mo e ce?

To form other question words, you take ce and then attach the kind of information you are asking for.

Try the pattern before seeing the little table.

DOM means place. What should CE + DOM ask?

Reveal **cedom** = **where?**

Now another one:

LI means time. What should CE + LI ask?

Reveal **celi** = **when?**

The core set is:

Form Built from Meaning ce — what? cei CE + EI person who? cedom CE + DOM place where? celi CE + LI time when?

These four cover most of what you'll need here. The rest of the question family follows the same pattern.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: DOM — place. Mnemonic: domicile; Latin/Romance domus. LI — time. Mnemonic: lifetime / timeline. NON — path, way, manner. Mnemonic: moving on and on along a path. GE — finances. Mnemonic: get / give money. ILI — cognition. Mnemonic: illuminate an idea; intelligence. FOU — lack. Mnemonic: few — you need something when you have too little of it.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown gedom bank GE finances + DOM place wanon swim WA water + NON path ilian know ILI cognition + AN action anifou need ANI movement toward + FOU lack

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

anvu = go boemo = cook mo = eat / food

cedom i anvu?

Click to Reveal Translation *Where are you going?*

i anvu en gedom

Click to Reveal Translation *I am going to / at the bank.*

celi i anvu?

Click to Reveal Translation *When are you going?*

cei i boemo?

Click to Reveal Translation *Who is cooking?*

e ce i anifou?

Click to Reveal Translation *What do you need?*

i ilianum

Click to Reveal Translation *I do not know.*

i wanon

Click to Reveal Translation *I swim.*

docs.title: Try it with someone
docs.text:
You can ask a real question now:

ce i mo? cedom i anvu? celi i anvu?

The Oravia Discord is a good place to try it out. Ask a question or write two sentences about yourself in the Discord, even if you need the dictionary.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text:
Four short connectors cover a lot of everyday speech:

su — and / with / also mai — but / however dou — or eta — so / therefore / then

Did you know? In Italian, ma, which is similar to mai, also means but; and in Portuguese, ou, which is similar to dou, also means or. For eta, you may think of ergo, which came to English from therefore in Latin.

nim su eofa i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *A friend and I go / I go with a friend.*

a wamu a yalgai, mai a leirih a yaltan

Click to Reveal Translation *The fish is small, but the tree is big.*

i mo dou i anefene?

Click to Reveal Translation *Are you eating or resting?*

nim i mo, eta i anefene

Click to Reveal Translation *I eat, then I rest.*

When two connected actions have the same obvious subject, you normally do not need to repeat the pronoun.

docs.title: SU also has a building-block meaning
docs.text:
You already know su as and / with / also. Its building-block meaning is alongside.

That gives you fasu:

fasu = FA family + SU alongside → sibling

Family members are expressed based on the generation. The sibling is the family member beside you in the same generation, that's why we say alongside.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: SU — alongside. Mnemonic: two things side by side. CO — communication. Mnemonic: communication. NI — new. Mnemonic: new / neo. RI — act. Mnemonic: a rite is an act. RO — thinking, reasoning. Mnemonic: reason. OI — fun, amusement. Mnemonic: Oi! as a lively exclamation.

docs.title: Words
docs.text:
Oravia Meaning Breakdown fasu sibling FA family + SU alongside leini seed LEI plants + NI new eori polite, courteous; please EO social + RI act anro decide AN action + RO thinking oico gossip OI fun + CO communication

Look at two of the breakdowns:

leini = plant + new → seed anro = action + reasoning → decide

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

ilian = know anona = give eofa = friend anefene = rest

eori, ce i mo?

Click to Reveal Translation *Please, what are you eating?*

nim fasu i ilian, mai nim i ilianum

Click to Reveal Translation *My sibling knows, but I do not know.*

i anona e leini u eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I give a seed to a friend.*

i anro, eta i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I decide, so I go.*

i oico su eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I gossip with a friend.*

i mo dou i anefene?

Click to Reveal Translation *Are you eating or resting?*

docs.title: CA connects a clause
docs.text:
Suppose you already have these two pieces:

i ilian — I know run i anvu — you go

Put ca before the second clause:

i ilian ca run i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I know that you are going.*

The first I is left unstated because you are talking about yourself. run stays in the second clause because its subject is different.

Notice the pair:

ce asks for information. ca connects information.

Spot the pair

You know celi = when? What would you expect cali to mean?

Reveal

cali = when in a statement.

One useful extension is cali:

cali = CA + LI time → when

i anefene cali run i boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *I rest when you cook.*

The other CA forms follow the same pattern of changing ce to ca. You'll meet more of them later. ca and cali are already enough to build much longer sentences.

docs.title: Numbers 1–5
docs.text:
tam — 1 tor — 2 par — 3 bale — 4 alui — 5

Nouns still do not change for plural:

tam eofa = one friend par eofa = three friends

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: ILA — sharing information. Mnemonic: “I'lL Announce it.” LUAN — tongue. Mnemonic: Spanish lengua, Portuguese língua, English language. MOA — fruits. Mnemonic: Mango, Orange, Apple. LEN — long. Mnemonic: length / longitude. DAI — desire, want. Mnemonic: desire.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown ilaluan say, tell ILA sharing information + LUAN tongue moalen banana MOA fruit + LEN long anidai want ANI movement toward + DAI desire apavu run APA physical movement + VU movement

docs.title: Try ilidai
docs.text:
You already know ILI = cognition. This lesson gives you DAI = desire.

What does ilidai make you think of? We don't expect you to be able to guess new words correctly, but thinking about it may help you remember them.

Reveal **ilidai** = **intention**.

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

ilian = know anvu = go leirih = tree yaltan = big eofa = friend

i ilian ca run i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I know that you are going.*

i ilaluan ca a leirih a yaltan

Click to Reveal Translation *I say that the tree is big.*

i anidai e par moalen, mai i mo e tam moalen

Click to Reveal Translation *I want three bananas, but I eat one banana.*

i apavu cali eofa i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I run when a friend goes.*

par eofa i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *Three friends go.*

docs.title: Lesson 9: Verb Stacking, Numbers 6–10, and NE Gradation
Verb stacking
docs.text:
When one verb leads into another, repeat i before the next verb:

i [first verb] i [second verb]

For several very common verbs, the first verb normally appears as its short form. This is simply the root of the verb, without the initial word cluster:

Full word Short form in a stack Meaning anidai dai want anifou fou need ando do can

i dai i boemo

Click to Reveal Translation *I want to cook.*

i fou i anefene

Click to Reveal Translation *I need to rest.*

i do i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I can go.*

docs.title: Numbers 6–10
docs.text:
teva — 6 peri — 7 auta — 8 tenda — 9 das — 10

Did you know oito, which sounds a bit like auta, is eight in Portuguese? And dez, which sounds a bit like das, is ten?

Larger numbers put the larger unit first:

das tam = 11 das alui = 15 tor das = 20 par das bale = 34

docs.title: NE gradation: rate it from 0 to 10
docs.text:
NE turns a number into a degree scale, always with 10 as reference. Put ne + number before something that can naturally vary by degree. For example, let's use ne gradation with the adjective difficult:

nealui yudur — 5/10 difficult → moderately difficult neauta yudur — 8/10 difficult → very difficult nedas yudur — 10/10 difficult → extremely difficult

The scale can include zero as sunya:

nesunya — 0/10, not at all

And it can go beyond ten when you want an “over the scale” reading:

nedastam yudur — 11/10 difficult → too difficult / excessively difficult

The same scale gives you a little, halfway, very, completely, and every point in between.

Notice that this can be used for frequency, likelihood, and many others. This system gives precision while avoiding adding dozens of words (such as rather, often and certain) to the core vocabulary.

Try it

yaltan = big, large. If auta = 8, what does neauta yaltan suggest?

Reveal

8/10 big, roughly very big.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: WIL — human-made geography: settlements and built connections. Mnemonic: village / villa. VIS — organs. Mnemonic: viscera. WOL — wide. Mnemonic: wall-to-wall. NE — quantity and degree. Mnemonic: number.

docs.title: Words
docs.text:
Oravia Meaning Breakdown ando can, be able AN action + DO regulations (permission/possibility) wiltan city WIL human-made geography + TAN big vismo stomach VIS organs + MO eating yalwol wide YAL size/dimension + WOL wide

Look at wiltan and visomo:

wiltan = built geography + big → city visomo = organ + eating → stomach

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

dai / anidai = want fou / anifou = need boemo = cook anefene = rest beivu = car

i dai i boemo, mai i fou i anefene

Click to Reveal Translation *I want to cook, but I need to rest.*

a nim i ando i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *I can go. (full form)*

i do i anvu en beivu

Click to Reveal Translation *I can go by car.*

a wiltan a neauta yalwol

Click to Reveal Translation *The city is very wide.*

nim visomo i anifou e mo, eta nim i mo

Click to Reveal Translation *My stomach needs food, so I eat.*

docs.title: Lesson 10: AR & IS
docs.text: Oravia usually tells you when something happens with a time expression: yesterday, next week, or a general word such as lar and lis. The verb itself can stay plain.

docs.title: Start with the time expression
docs.text:
A few useful time expressions are:

litamar — yesterday litamis — tomorrow lar — once / at some unspecified time in the past lis — one day / at some unspecified time in the future

litamar, i mo e moalen

Click to Reveal Translation *Yesterday, I ate a banana.*

lis, i mo e moalen

Click to Reveal Translation *One day, I will eat a banana.*

The time word carries the past or future reference, so that mo itself stays bare.

docs.title: -ar and -is
docs.text:
Use -ar when an action is already complete by the time you are talking about:

i moar

Click to Reveal Translation *I have eaten / I already ate.*

Use -is when an action is still later than that point:

i mois

Click to Reveal Translation *I have not eaten yet / I am going to eat.*

With the present as the reference, these can look a little like past and future. The distinction becomes clearer when you compare two events.

A quick picture:

[ action-ar ] → reference point → [ action-is ]

-ar points to something already on the earlier/completed side. -is points to something still on the later/not-yet-started side.

docs.title: Before and after another event
docs.text:
Start with two events in the same past scene:

litamar, nim i mo cali haya i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *Yesterday, I was eating when they went.*

Now add -ar to the first event:

litamar, nim i moar cali haya i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *Yesterday, I had already eaten when they went.*

The eating is complete by the time of the going.

What changed?

Compare the two sentences. Everything is the same except mo → moar. That one suffix tells you the eating was already finished at the second event.

Or put -is on the second event:

litamar, nim i mo, haya i anvuis

Click to Reveal Translation *Yesterday, when I ate, they had not gone yet / they went later.*

Notice that this avoids a lot of complicated verb tenses in languages such as English.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: GEH (subcluster) — sales. Mnemonic: Goods Exchange Hands. YO — colors. Mnemonic: Yellow, Orange. YAR — light. Mnemonic: RAY backwards. LEA — landscape. Mnemonic: English lea, “meadow.” REL — up, high. Mnemonic: rise / elevate.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown gehna buy GEH sales + NA giving yoyar white YO colors + YAR light leayo garden LEA landscape + YO colors iliro think ILI cognition + RO thinking borel ceiling BOR house structure + REL up/high

docs.title: Try liyar
docs.text:
You already knew LI = time. Now you know YAR = light.

What time of day does liyar suggest?

Reveal **liyar** = **morning, daytime**.

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

moalen = banana anvu = go cali = when

litamar, i mo e moalen

Click to Reveal Translation *Yesterday, I ate a banana.*

a borel a yoyar

Click to Reveal Translation *The ceiling is white.*

i iliro ca a leayo a yaltan

Click to Reveal Translation *I think the garden is big.*

litamis, nim i boemoar cali haya i mo

Click to Reveal Translation *Tomorrow, I will have already cooked when they eat (cooking, with -ar, completed by the time of the other action).*

lis, i anvu en leayo

Click to Reveal Translation *One day, I will go to the garden.*

docs.title: Lesson 11: Compounds, Hyphens, and Imports
docs.text: What if the word you need isn't in the dictionary?

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text: So far you've mostly worked inside words: BOE + MO → boemo. You can also combine whole words.

docs.title: Ordinary modifier: describe this particular thing
docs.text:
yoyar beivu

Click to Reveal Translation *a white car*

Here yoyar just describes this car.

docs.title: Compound: make one concept
docs.text:
To indicate that the words together create a category or concept, we add -s to the modifier. We may also add sol before the compound to make it extra explicit, but that's optional.

Now imagine a vehicle that is basically a kitchen on wheels:

sol boemos beivu

Click to Reveal Translation *kitchen-vehicle → a food truck*

The -s marks compound words except for the last. sol announces to the listener that a compound is coming.

You can still describe that food truck:

yoyar sol boemos beivu

Click to Reveal Translation *a white food truck*

yoyar describes this particular one. sol boemos beivu names the kind of vehicle.

docs.title: Hyphen: blend two meanings
docs.text:
With a hyphen, one word is coloring the meaning of another. It is usually done with verbs to give them more nuance and expression, and make sentences more direct:

i eori-ilaluan u eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I speak politely / courteously to a friend.*

Here ilaluan is still the main action, and eori gives it the polite flavor.

docs.title: Imports and local coinages
docs.text:
A word outside the official vocabulary begins with an apostrophe:

'Italia — Italy 'Nihongo — Japanese language

Use the apostrophe for names and other words brought in from outside the fixed Oravia vocabulary: places, dishes, languages, species, local coinages, and so on.

docs.title: Before you split a word apart
docs.text: A root can be more than one syllable. FENE, LUAN, PILI, and REVA are each single roots, so they don't split further. The same letters may also do different jobs in different words. There are only about ~260 building blocks, and once learned, recognizing them becomes easy.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: CIU — creative products. Mnemonic: create. REVA — accurate, real. Mnemonic: real / verify. MIR — lots, much, many. Mnemonic: myriad. SOI — speed. Mnemonic: Sprint Out Immediately. VIO — change. Mnemonic: variation. PILI — delicate. Mnemonic: picture a delicate petal.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown ciureva photo, picture CIU creative product + REVA accurate/real lumirwa flood LU outside/weather + MIR lots + WA water lisoi soon LI time + SOI speed leipili flower LEI plants + PILI delicate

docs.title: Six words you were never taught
docs.text: You've learned enough building blocks to try six dictionary words that never appeared in the lessons. See what you make of them before clicking.

docs.title: 1. wilgai
docs.text:
WIL human-made geography + GAI small → wilgai = ?

Reveal **village / town**

docs.title: 2. visro
docs.text:
VIS organs + RO thinking → visro = ?

Reveal **brain**

docs.title: 3. lealei
docs.text:
LEA landscape + LEI plants → lealei = ?

Reveal **forest**

docs.title: 4. wilyel
docs.text:
WIL human-made geography + YEL joining → wilyel = ?

Reveal **bridge**

docs.title: 5. apasoi
docs.text:
APA physical movement + SOI speed → apasoi = ?

Reveal **hurry / rush**

docs.title: 6. oipili
docs.text:
OI fun + PILI delicate → oipili = ?

Reveal **cute / adorable**

With the building blocks from this short course, more than 40 additional dictionary words have breakdowns made entirely from pieces you already know.

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

leayo = garden eori = polite / please ilaluan = say / tell eofa = friend lis = one day / sometime in the future

i anona e ciureva u eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I give a photo to a friend.*

a lumirwa a yaltan

Click to Reveal Translation *The flood is big.*

lisoi, i anvu en leayo

Click to Reveal Translation *Soon, I go to the garden.*

a leipili en leayo

Click to Reveal Translation *The flower is in the garden.*

sol boemos beivu

Click to Reveal Translation *kitchen-vehicle → food truck*

i eori-ilaluan u eofa

Click to Reveal Translation *I speak politely to a friend.*

lis, i anvu en 'Italia

Click to Reveal Translation *One day, I will go to Italy.*

docs.text: Make a compound, a hyphenated expression, or a marked import. Pick whichever one sounds fun.

docs.text:
Quick review:

docs.title: Lesson 12: Conditionals and where to go next
docs.text: One last piece of grammar: two useful ways to say if.

docs.title: Daefer: if this is the case...
docs.text:
Use daefer for a real possibility or cause-and-effect condition.

daefer run i anvu, i anvu su

Click to Reveal Translation *If you go, I go too.*

docs.title: Iliciu: imagine this instead...
docs.text:
iliciu means imagine. It sets up a hypothetical or counterfactual situation.

iliciu a nim a run, i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *If I were you, I would go.*

Notice that by using daefer or iliciu, we avoid many complicated verb forms in other languages such as English.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: ELI — virtue. Mnemonic: Ethical Living Ideals. VER — safety, security. Mnemonic: French verrou, a lock or bolt. ELO — social virtues. Mnemonic: Portuguese elo, a link or bond.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Oravia Meaning Breakdown elireva truth, true ELI virtue + REVA accurate/real anever secure, safe ANE static action + VER safety eloele freedom, free ELO social virtues + ELE self-expansion iliciu imagine ILI cognition + CIU creative product

docs.title: Put it together
docs.text:
From earlier lessons

beivu = car do / ando = can ciureva = photo anidai = want eleyel = love yudur = difficult

daefer a beivu a anever, i do i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *If the car is safe, I can go.*

iliciu a nim a run, i anro, eta i anvu

Click to Reveal Translation *If I were you, I would decide and then go.*

i ilian ca a ciureva a elireva

Click to Reveal Translation *I know that the picture is accurate / true to reality.*

i eleyel e eloele

Click to Reveal Translation *I love freedom.*

docs.title: How much Oravia do you know now?
docs.text:
Oravia is fast to learn, and it was designed with a purposefully small vocabulary that is very powerful combined with the grammatical and expressive features of the language. It has about ~860 dictionary words built mostly from ~260 building blocks. In these twelve lessons you've met about 65 building blocks, roughly a quarter of the building-block system.

The six words in Lesson 11 were never taught as vocabulary. More than 40 other dictionary words also have breakdowns made entirely from pieces in this short course.

docs.title: The simple form is usually enough
docs.text:
This course has mostly used Oravia's simple core.

When you need more precision, you can add it: mark singular or plural explicitly, distinguish moving into a place from moving toward it, or make other distinctions that these twelve lessons haven't covered. Most everyday sentences work fine with the simple form. The philosophy is a simple system that has options for disambiguation or more precision if needed.

docs.title: Final reading
docs.text:
Everything below has appeared somewhere in the course, including a few words you worked out in Lesson 11.

Read as much as you can first. If a word has slipped your mind, open the reading tips without revealing the translation.

Reading tips

lis — one day / sometime in the future eofa — friend anvu — go wiltan — city lealei — forest yalwol — wide leirih — tree yaltan — big leipili — flower oipili — cute ilaluan — say / tell eleyel — love visomo — stomach anifou — need mo — food / eat apasoi — hurry lisoi — soon anona — give fasu — sibling

Lis, nim su eofa i anvu de wiltan en lealei. A lealei a yalwol, su a leirih a yaltan. En lealei, a leipili a oipili. Eofa i ilaluan ca hay i eleyel e lealei. Nim visomo i anifou e mo, eta nim i apasoi. Lisoi, nim su eofa i anvu en wiltan. En wiltan, i anona e leipili u fasu. Fasu i ilaluan ca a leipili a oipili.

Reveal the reading

One day, my friend and I go from the city to the forest. The forest is wide, and the tree is big. In the forest, a flower is cute. My friend says that they love the forest. My stomach needs food, so I hurry. Soon, my friend and I go to the city. In the city, I give the flower to my sibling. My sibling says that the flower is cute.

docs.text:
If you only know what's in this Primer, that's already enough to start. Join the Discord and write a few lines in Oravia: introduce yourself, say something about your day, ask a question, or reply to someone else. Use the dictionary as much as you need.

docs.title: Keep going
docs.text:
You can use Oravia now. Read something, write a few lines about your day, or make a ridiculous compound.

If you continue into the Complete Course, a lot will already be familiar, but more in-depth. Because of that, you may go faster if something feels easy, but I recommend that you start from the beginning. As you explore further, there will be more to discover such as changing clusters of words or adding speaker stances.

docs.title: Lusaria
docs.text:
Lusaria is a main city in Oravia. It is located in the North, by a warm sea. It is comprised of the coast plus many islands.

Lusaria is a cosmopolitan confederation with a liberal government (based on contracts, rules and individual rights). The main activities include fishing, trading, bureaucracy, and scholarship. They have a thousand-year-old scholar tradition with impressive universities, libraries and telescope towers, and the main fields that thrive there are astronomy, sorcery, and law. The scholarship there being so old is one of the reasons scholars write in a different script, by the way. The Stars Script used to be common in long gone eras.

Lusaria does not have much of a military tradition, but it is well protected by a navy, sorcerers, and natural barriers (there is a mountainous terrain surrounding it inland, and a rock/coral barrier in the sea). It also does not hurt they have a long diplomacy tradition and prosperous trade that other nations depend on.

[more worldbuilding coming soon :)]

docs.title: Script
docs.text:
We are now squarely outside of auxlang territory. Oravia also has scripts for worldbuilding purposes!

All scripts work the same way. They convey both sound and meaning, each word is exactly two symbols long, and there are only 21 unique letters.

How is that possible? You may wonder... Oravia's unique structure makes it possible!

docs.title: The structure
docs.text:
Before you proceed, a note: this explanation will make much more sense if you already know some Oravia!

It works like this: First symbol -> the domain First marker -> the cluster Second marker -> the subcluster Second symbol -> the sound

The symbols would be equivalent to letters. The markers on those symbols are equivalent to numbers. For example, if we want to say lunhem, summer. We would write the equivalent of:

L11H

L is the domain, nature. 1 is the cluster in that domain, lu. The order of clusters are the order they appear in the lessons, so 0 is li, 1 is lu and 2 is le. 1 is the subcluster within that cluster, lun. 0 would be base lu, 1 is lun, seasons. H is the sound. The last letter gives a sound clue. This works because by the time we narrow down to the subcluster, there are not a lot or word options.

So, L11H = lunhem

Then the prepositions, pronouns, etc, can be expressed based on domain sound, as in:

n = nim, r = run, d = de, s = su, etc

And they are accompanied by a marker which indicates they are not a "vocabulary" word.

docs.title: The Official Scripts
docs.text: There are two official scripts in Oravia.

docs.title: The Garden Script
docs.text: This is used by the government and official communication.

docs.title: The Stars Script
docs.text: This is used by astronomers, scholars and sorcerers.

docs.title: The Abujida
docs.text: This is a variation of the star and the garden scripts where the markers indicate vowels instead of cluster and subcluster. Used by traders, fishermen and laborers because it's simpler and more practical. It looks fairly similar to the official scripts, except that it uses more space (many syllables per word instead of just using two symbols), and words may be separated by dots or spaces.

docs.title: The Animal Crackers
docs.text:
This kind of script is used by children. The motifs are usually animals, plants and scenery, and that's where the name came from. Each child or group of children create their own, and they are constantly changing. Because of this, there are many variations and adults cannot read it.

Some examples of Animal Crackers Script
